claims.text: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni can have a single-phase FCC structure.
The equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets are also single-phase FCC after the same thermomechanical processing as the quinary alloy.
The controlled intervention is removal of one or two elements from Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni while holding thermomechanical processing constant.
Mechanical comparisons will be made under identical room-temperature uniaxial tensile or compression conditions.
Changing from the quinary alloy to its quaternary or ternary subsets changes local chemical short-range order and lattice distortion.
Local chemical short-range order and lattice distortion modify stacking-fault energy.
Lattice-parameter mismatch among constituents can hinder partial-dislocation motion through friction.
The quinary alloy has greater local lattice distortion and a more complex chemical environment than its reduced-component subsets.
The quinary alloy's chemical and lattice complexity promotes enhanced dislocation pinning.
Slip and deformation twinning can operate in single-phase FCC equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi during deformation near room temperature.
The quinary alloy has enhanced twinning activity relative to its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Removing one or more elements reduces local strain fields in the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Enhanced dislocation pinning and twinning in the quinary alloy produce greater yield strength and work hardening.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary subsets will have lower yield strength.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary subsets will have lower work-hardening rates.
The quaternary and ternary subsets will form fewer deformation twins because they have a more homogeneous local chemical environment and higher effective stacking-fault energies.
The proposed comparison is limited to single-phase FCC samples without secondary precipitates and without significant texture differences.
The quantitative effects of particular elemental interactions on short-range order and stacking-fault energy are not well established.
Comparable ordering and stacking-fault energies across all compositions, or absence of the predicted quinary advantages in strength, work hardening, and twinning, would falsify the hypothesis.
